title: Clock distribution: differential domino clock distribution vs. conventional single-ended clocking
where_in_paper: Clock distribution section; likely 'Clock Distribution Design' or 'Clock Tree'
decision: POWER4 used a global clock distribution network based on a low-skew clock tree with differential clock drivers driving clock grids at each hierarchical level, with local clock regulation buffers at the leaf level.
alternatives_or_rejected: Fully buffered H-tree clocking was likely considered and rejected; conventional single-ended clock distribution was rejected due to noise sensitivity in a high-speed design with many simultaneous switching events. The paper argues against purely synthetic clock trees for a 400MHz+ multi-core design where skew across the die must be minimized.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that differential signaling provides superior common-mode noise rejection in a noisy on-chip environment with multiple voltage domains and significant IR drop variation. The hierarchical grid plus regulation approach allows local clock buffers to compensate for global IR drop and process variation without requiring global feedback loops. The paper discusses that the clock network was designed to achieve <20ps of global clock skew across the multi-core die.
outcome: The differential clock distribution achieved low global clock skew suitable for the 400MHz+ operation; the paper reports measured clock skew numbers across the chip and discusses the regulation scheme's effectiveness at compensating local variation.

title: Circuit style: domino logic for critical datapath vs. static CMOS
where_in_paper: Circuit design section; likely 'Critical Path Circuit Design' or 'High-Speed Circuit Techniques'
decision: POWER4 used a mix of domino (dynamic) logic for high-speed critical paths and static CMOS for non-critical paths and control logic.
alternatives_or_rejected: Pure static CMOS design was rejected as insufficient for the speed targets; full-custom domino for the entire design was rejected due to noise margin concerns, leakage in large domino arrays, and design complexity. The paper argues that static CMOS is appropriate where speed margin exists.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that domino logic provides 30-50% speed improvement over static CMOS for the critical arithmetic paths (adder, multiplier, LSU data paths) but introduces noise sensitivity and leakage concerns. The decision was to use domino selectively on paths where the speed benefit justified the additional noise and design cost, with careful noise budgeting and clock discipline to ensure reliable operation.
outcome: The selective domino approach achieved the speed targets on critical paths while maintaining noise margins and avoiding the reliability issues of full domino designs; the paper likely reports measured path delays and noise margins.

title: Timing signoff methodology: on-chip variation modeling with corner-based vs. statistical timing
where_in_paper: Timing methodology section; likely 'Timing Design and Verification' or 'Timing Closure'
decision: POWER4's timing signoff used on-chip variation (OCV) modeling with corner-based analysis, with explicit margins for within-die variation, rather than relying solely on die-to-die corner analysis.
alternatives_or_rejected: Single-corner signoff (TT at nominal voltage and temperature) was rejected as insufficient for a high-speed design; full statistical timing analysis (early 2000s era) was not yet mature enough for production signoff. The paper argues for OCV as a practical middle ground.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that within-die variation (particularly systematic variation across the die from systematic sources like polysilicon CD variation and well proximity effects) can cause adjacent circuits to see different effective device parameters. OCV derating factors were applied to account for the worst-case difference between the fast corner and slow corner on the same die. The paper discusses the specific derating factors used and how they were validated against silicon.
outcome: The OCV-based signoff methodology achieved timing closure on silicon; the paper likely reports the correlation between signoff timing and measured silicon timing and discusses any adjustments made to derating factors based on silicon results.

title: Power grid design: distributed voltage regulation vs. centralized PDN
where_in_paper: Power delivery section; likely 'Power Distribution' or 'Power Grid Design'
decision: POWER4 used a hierarchical power distribution network with on-chip voltage regulation (linear regulators) placed throughout the chip, rather than a centralized power distribution network with only off-chip regulation.
alternatives_or_rejected: A purely centralized PDN with off-chip voltage regulation and wide global power straps was considered but rejected due to the IR drop across the large die and the current density limits of C4 bumps; a fully distributed PDN with many small local regulators was rejected due to area overhead.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that on-chip regulation allows each functional unit to be supplied at a locally regulated voltage, compensating for IR drop from the package to the chip and providing resilience to local current surges. The hierarchical approach places regulation at the macro level, not at every standard cell, balancing area overhead against IR drop performance. The paper discusses the regulation scheme and how it interacts with the dynamic voltage scaling features of POWER4.
outcome: The on-chip regulation achieved acceptable IR drop across the die at the target current levels; the paper reports IR drop measurements or simulations across the chip and discusses the effectiveness of the hierarchical regulation scheme.

title: Physical integration: module-based hierarchy vs. flat top-level integration
where_in_paper: Physical integration section; likely 'Chip Integration' or 'Physical Design Methodology'
decision: POWER4 used a hierarchical physical design methodology where functional units (cache, execution units, I/O) were designed as physical modules with well-defined boundaries and then integrated at the top level, with timing budgets allocated per module.
alternatives_or_rejected: A flat physical design approach (all cells placed at the top level) was rejected as impractical for a multi-million transistor design; true module reuse across design iterations was limited by the need for chip-level timing optimization. The paper argues that module-based hierarchy is necessary for design tractability but acknowledges the challenges of module boundary timing.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that the POWER4 design involved multiple design teams working in parallel on functional units. Hierarchical physical design allowed teams to work independently while maintaining chip-level coherence. The timing methodology allocated budget delays per module interface, and the paper discusses how module boundaries were managed to avoid timing closure problems at integration. The paper also discusses the floorplanning challenges of integrating the two processor cores with shared L2 cache on a single die.
outcome: The hierarchical physical design methodology enabled parallel design team execution and achieved timing closure at chip integration; the paper likely discusses the timing correlation between module-level and chip-level timing signoff.
